growth_story.headline: After decades of slow, uneven gains, Benin's income per person sped up to 3.7 percent a year from 2017 as reforms and investment took hold.
growth_story.arc: From 1990 to 2016 Benin's income per person grew slowly and unevenly, at 1.3 percent a year, rising from about 749 to 1,006 dollars in constant prices. The sources describe an economy that leaned on cotton and on transit trade with Nigeria. That left it exposed to its big neighbour's policies and held back more productive manufacturing and services. From 2017 growth stepped up to 3.7 percent a year, and the last decade averaged 3.4 against 1.2 in the decade before. The IMF ties the turn to a reform programme launched in 2016 and a public building drive, and investment rose from 19.7 percent of GDP in 2016 to 35.4 in 2025. Growth stayed positive even in 2020, at 1.1, and reached 5.5 in 2025, when income per person hit its highest level on record.

threads.title: Cotton and the Nigeria trade
threads.text: For decades Benin earned its living from a few crops, mainly cotton, and from goods passing through its port to Nigeria. The World Bank says this reliance held back more productive manufacturing and services. It also left Benin exposed when Nigeria closed its border in 2019 and 2020.

threads.title: A reform and building drive
threads.text: Since 2016 the government has run a reform programme alongside a public building drive. The IMF links this to faster and steadier growth. Investment climbed from 19.7 percent of GDP in 2016 to 35.4 in 2025.

threads.title: Processing crops at home
threads.text: A special economic zone opened in 2020 to process farm goods in Benin rather than ship them raw. A textile plant there is meant to handle every step from ginned cotton onward.

citations.quote: The authorities launched a special economic zone (SEZ) in 2020, with some factories already operational for local transformation of commodities.

citations.quote: The integrated textile unit in the SEZ is expected to cover every step of the transformation process of cotton lint ginned by local factories.

threads.title: Trouble on the borders
threads.text: Benin's neighbours remain a source of shocks. The closure of the border with Niger cut port traffic in 2023, and fragility persists in the north and the wider region. Even so, the country has kept unbroken constitutional rule.

citations.title: Benin: Staff Report for the 2024 Article IV Consultation, Fourth Review Under the Extended Fund Facility and the Extended Credit Facility Arrangements (IMF Country Report No. 24/338)
citations.quote: The service sector was buoyed by retail trade and tourism, partially compensating for the sharp drop in port activity amid the Niger border closure.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Benin

threads.title: A young population
threads.text: Benin's population is very young. The World Bank says growth has done little for living standards so far, and productivity remains low.

since_last_year.text: Growth held up through the 2026 election year. Income per person rose 5.5 percent in 2025, its fastest pace since 1990, and a new government took office in May 2026. The World Bank says the vote and the Middle East conflict did little to slow activity.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Benin
citations.quote: The government formed by the two main ruling parties took office in May 2026.

citations.title: Macro Poverty Outlook: Benin
citations.quote: The Middle East conflict and electoral cycle have had limited effects on economic activity.

growth_story.tension: The sources report growth for the whole economy, which has run well above growth in income per person. Income per person grew 3.7 percent a year from 2017 and 5.5 in 2025, as a fast-growing population shares the gains. The World Bank adds that strong growth has done little to cut poverty.
